newsitem.title: USA: Merrill Lynch sees $2 CSCE coffee by mid-1997.
newsitem.headline: Merrill Lynch sees $2 CSCE coffee by mid-1997.

text.p: Merrill Lynch said a tighter supply situation could drive arabica coffee futures to as high as 200.00 cents a lb ($2) by mid-1997.

"We are looking at a radical change in our fundamantal analysis of this market," Merrill Lynch said in its bi-monthly report. "Rather than prices dropping this quarter, we now believe we could be on the verge of a major move up."

The report, dated Jan 21, said an increased flow of new crop coffee out of South America and heavy producer selling suggested that the first quarter of 1997 would bring some relief to the market and even spur a slight build-up in consummer inventories. But aggressive purchasing by European roasters had absorbed the new crop supply of coffee and caused U.S. inventories to dwindle.
"Total supplies have not been this tight in 20 years," the report said. "Although it is hard to prove statistically, we believe Arabica supplies might be the tightest on record."
Merrill Lynch said the market outlook hinged on the Brazilian 1997/98 coffee harvest and the response of the Brazilian government to release holdings should the crop be reduced.
"If Brazil truly has a small harvest, $2.00 coffee by mid-year would not be out of the question," it said.

Preliminary forecasts by the Brazilian government have pegged the country's 1997/98 coffee crop between 18 million and 20 million 60-kg bags compared with an estimated 25 million bags the previous season.
But the market has been in denial of these estimates and is not likely to respond to this factor until a non-Brazilian sources, such as USDA, supports these claims, Merrill said.
Merrill said it would have anticipated a further recovery of the Brazilian crop following a severe frost in 1994, but unusually heavy rainfall may have inhibited the fruit set.

"Even if production in Brazil were to drop 3-4 million bags rather than the 7-8 million bag drop now being touted, this would still put the market in a very precarious state and cause Arabica supplies to contract even further," it said.
Stocks of coffee certified against the CSCE were at extremely low levels, it noted. As of Jan 20, U.S. certified coffee stocks stood at 22,363 60-kg bags, the CSCE reported.
Reductions in U.S. coffee inventories have not been matched by a corresponding drop in European stocks, which has put pressure on London LIFFE coffee futures.

However, a possible change in the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) quota plan could restrict the shipment of robustas and lead to a reduction in robusta inventories, Merrill Lynch said.
The ACPC council will meet in Rio de Janeiro on Thursday to consider an African proposal calling for an export cut of 2.5 million 60-kg bags in the first half of 1997 to lock in higher prices.
An African plan envisaged a reduction of 1.0 million tonnes in robusta exports and 1.5 million in arabicas. ((-- Patricia Avidan, New York Commodities Desk 212 859 1640))
